answer:
No. According to your records, you are not supposed to be taking lisinopril any more. Dr. Elena Marsh stopped it on September 22, 2025 because it gave you a dry cough, and she started losartan 50 mg once a day in its place. At your December 9, 2025 visit the cough had gone away. The hospital's latest summary (March 2026) also shows lisinopril as discontinued on September 22, 2025 and losartan as your current blood pressure medicine. Your pharmacy's list (July 2026) has no lisinopril on it, and your losartan was last filled on June 28, 2026.

The app is most likely showing an older copy of your hospital records, from before the change. Those older copies (2023 to mid-2025) list lisinopril as active, and they were never updated in the app. Please don't restart lisinopril because of the app. Your clinic also lists lisinopril cough as an intolerance, so if you are asked about drug reactions, include it. If you still have lisinopril tablets at home, don't take them. Losartan and lisinopril are not meant to be taken together.

Two things to bring up with Dr. Marsh or your pharmacist. First, ask them to correct or remove the lisinopril entry in the app. Second, I noticed a separate medicine mismatch. The hospital stopped hydrochlorothiazide on March 5, 2026 after you were admitted with a low sodium level. Your clinic's June 2026 list and your pharmacy's list still show it as active, and the pharmacy filled it on April 2, 2026. Your sodium was still slightly low (134) on June 15, 2026. Please check with Dr. Marsh whether you should be taking hydrochlorothiazide.
short: Lisinopril was stopped on 22 Sept 2025 for a dry cough and replaced by losartan 50 mg daily. Any record still listing it as active is out of date. Separately, hydrochlorothiazide was stopped in the hospital in March 2026 for low sodium but is still active at the clinic and pharmacy, and needs clarifying.

knowledge.says: Dry cough is a common side effect of ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril. Switching to an angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan is the usual approach, and it keeps the blood pressure benefit without the cough.
knowledge.guideline: ACC/AHA hypertension guideline: use an ARB when an ACE inhibitor causes cough.

items.says: Lisinopril and losartan shouldn't be taken together.
items.why: Both lower blood pressure by acting on the same hormone system. Combining them raises the risk of high potassium and kidney problems, so only one of them is used.

knowledge.says: Dual blockade of the renin-angiotensin system, with an ACE inhibitor plus an ARB, increases hyperkalemia, low blood pressure and kidney injury without added benefit in most people.
knowledge.guideline: ACC/AHA hypertension guideline advises against combining an ACE inhibitor and an ARB.
